newsitem.title: NORWAY: Study says Norwegians most depressed in winter.
newsitem.headline: Study says Norwegians most depressed in winter.

text.p: Norway has the world's highest incidence of depression related to the cold, dark conditions of winter, a psychologist said on Saturday.

On average, more than 20 percent of Norwegians suffer depression and related symptoms during winter, but the rate can reach up to 27 percent in some parts of the far north, according to Arne Holte, psychology professor at Tromsoe University.
Between five and 10 percent were so seriously affected that they required treatment.

For more than 10 years specialists have been researching the link between light and a syndrome known as Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), which is characterised by recurrent depression at the onset of autumn and lasting until spring.
"Norway provides the best laboratory in the world for such an investigation," Holte told Reuters at a conference on SAD.

About 100 doctors from around the world have gathered in Tromsoe for the two-day meeting to find ways to beat SAD, which some psychiatrists say disrupts the lives of millions of unwitting sufferers from North America to Australia.
Norway is a narrow country stretching across 14 lines of latitude from Kristiansand on the south coast at 58 degrees north to North Cape at 71 degrees deep within the Arctic Circle.

Winters in Norway are long and hard and inhabitants in northerly regions are shrouded in darkness 24 hours a day from late November to the end of January. In the summer between May and July, the sun does not set.
In the biggest survey of its kind, Holte questioned 6,300 nursing and teaching students aged between 20 and 50 years nationwide over a two-week period in January 1993.

"We found the highest prevalence of winter depression ever measured in the world," Holte said. "There was a lower frequency of SAD-related symptoms in the southern parts of Norway and a much higher frequency in the northern regions."

He emphasised that it was not always easy to differentiate between SAD and another form of depression related to darkness and the production of the hormone melatonin in the brain's pineal gland, known as delayed sleep phase syndrome.
"Some will suffer delayed sleep phase syndrome and some will have SAD. Some may have a combination of the two," Holte said.
